planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or shortly after bloom in late summer; keep rhizomes shallow and never let them dry out.

directions: A ruffled, double-form Japanese iris with pale blue-violet petals overlaid by darker blue-violet veins and white signal markings near the throat, giving a frosted, two-tone effect. Flowers open wide and flat on tall, sturdy stems in early to midsummer, well above the strap-like foliage. Like all Japanese iris, it wants consistently moist, acidic soil and thrives at pond margins or in a bog bed; avoid lime and winter waterlogging in cold climates. Divide every 3-4 years after bloom to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or shortly after bloom; keep roots constantly moist through establishment.

directions: One of the clearest pure-pink Japanese iris cultivars bred, with large, single, rounded falls that open nearly flat in a soft rose-pink with minimal veining. Plants are early-blooming and heavily budded, carrying five to seven buds per stem for an extended flowering display. Grow in full sun with wet feet during the growing season, in rich, acidic, organic soil; it tolerates shallow standing water at pond edges. Mulch in cold-winter zones and avoid letting the crowns dry out, which quickly weakens Japanese iris clumps.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring; provide steady moisture while new roots establish.

directions: A near-true-blue Japanese iris with ruffled, flared petals that are medium blue at the center with darker veining, fading to pale blue to near-white at the margins, and light blue style arms with feathered crests. Blooms open wide in midseason on tall stems above arching, sword-like foliage. Best in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive, slightly acidic soil, and tolerant of shallow standing water during the growing season. Divide every few years in spring to keep clumps blooming freely.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring; keep consistently wet through the first season to establish.

directions: A striking bicolor Japanese iris with white petals washed by a large dark red-violet halo and branching red-violet veins radiating out to the ruffled edges, centered on a bold yellow signal patch. Blooms open flat and wide in early to midseason above clumps of narrow, upright foliage. Grow in full sun to light shade with constantly moist, acidic, humus-rich soil; it is well suited to pond margins and rain gardens. Lift and divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or late summer; Siberian iris resents root disturbance, so divide only when clumps decline.

directions: A tetraploid Siberian iris with delicately layered coloring: very light pink-lavender standards edged in a thin red line, light lavender-and-pink style arms with an aqua midrib, and light blue falls bordered by a wide red rim over dark blue veins, all centered on a ruffled cream-to-yellow signal. Blooms open in early midseason on sturdy, well-branched stems above grassy, clump-forming foliage. Unlike the boggier Japanese iris, Siberian iris tolerates average garden soil but performs best with regular moisture and full sun. Clumps are long-lived and rarely need division.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or late summer; established clumps can be left undisturbed for many years.

directions: A compact, richly colored Siberian iris with deep wine-purple falls edged in buttery gold and veined in near-black, paired with light lavender-blue standards and style arms that shimmer against the dark falls. Flowers are smaller than typical Siberian iris, around 2.5-3 inches across, but intricately marked and jewel-like, carried on short, stocky, vigorous stems. Grows well in average to moist garden soil and full sun to light shade, making it easier to place in a mixed border than true bog-grown iris. Its compact habit suits smaller gardens or front-of-border plantings.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or late summer; this compact cultivar is well suited to smaller beds and containers at the water's edge.

directions: A dwarf, multicolored Siberian iris with light lavender standards flushed rose at the base, rose-violet falls deepening to dark rose-violet near a double-lobed chartreuse signal outlined in dark blue-violet, and turquoise style arms that add a cool contrasting accent. Its shorter stature makes it stand out among taller Siberian iris cultivars, blooming midseason to late season. Grows readily in average to moist, humus-rich garden soil in full sun, and its compact size suits edging a pond or border front. Established clumps need little care beyond occasional division when flowering declines.

planting.note: Divide and transplant in early spring or late summer; established clumps are long-lived and rarely need dividing.

directions: An unusually warm-toned Siberian iris in shades of apricot, copper-red, and yellow rather than the typical blues and purples of the species. Pale standards are overlaid with red-violet veins and dappling, style arms are light apricot with a bright red-violet heart, and apricot falls are heavily speckled red around a bright yellow signal, with a light sweet fragrance. Blooms open in mid-season above a dense, tidy clump of grassy foliage that stays attractive through the season. Grows readily in average to moist garden soil in full sun and needs little maintenance once established.
